errors: No mathematical errors found; all boundary values checked are exact.
The page's '279' (in '-279', '9Y-14X=279/i', '18Y-28X=279') should read 277 = N(9+14i); the image is consistent with 277 and all derived values require it. The '/i' is likely '/2'.

results.what: Explicit description of the quarter system {0<Re(z/pi)<1/2, 0<Im(z/pi)<1/2} for pi = 9+14i via its four bounding lines, and row-by-row counting of its lattice points (69 = (N(pi)-1)/4).
results.modern_name: Biquadratic (quartic) analogue of Gauss's lemma / quarter system of residues; lattice-point counting in Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass on biquadratic residues, c. 1810s-1830s); lattice-point proofs of quartic reciprocity later published by Eisenstein (1844) and Busche (1880s)

results.what: Staircase/floor-function enumeration of lattice points under lines of slope 14/9 and -9/14 with alternating +1/-1 marks
results.modern_name: Counting lattice points under a line (Eisenstein-type floor sums)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (third proof of quadratic reciprocity, 1808), Eisenstein (1844 geometric version)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a worked numerical example of the quarter-system and lattice-point approach to biquadratic residues mod 9+14i. Gauss's Nachlass is known to contain this approach. The page is a nice concrete instance but not a new result.

checkable.asserts: the (28) column values are 28X on line Im(z/pi)=1/2
the (18) column values are 18X on line Re(z/pi)=1/2
top vertex of quarter square is -2.5+11.5i = -70/28+11.5i = -45/18+11.5i

checkable.sympy: sum(1 for X in range(-20,20) for Y in range(-20,20) if 0 < 9*X+14*Y < Rational(277,2) and 0 < 9*Y-14*X < Rational(277,2)) == 69
checkable.asserts: the quarter system mod 9+14i contains (277-1)/4 = 69 lattice points
